title: Design a Rate Limiter
summary: Four algorithms, and the interview is decided by whether you can name what each one gets wrong. Fixed windows let through double the limit at the boundary — if you cannot explain that, nothing else you say lands.

blocks.title: What you are actually being asked
blocks.text: Not *“implement a rate limiter”* — anyone can. **Which** algorithm, and **what it gets wrong**. Every one of the four has a failure mode, and picking one without naming its failure is the answer that does not get you hired.
Allow at most *N* requests per client per time window. Answer `allow(clientId)` in O(1), using memory proportional to the number of active clients rather than the number of requests.

items.title: Per client, per endpoint, or both?
items.text: The key shape decides your memory. `client:endpoint` multiplies state by the number of endpoints.

items.title: Is a burst acceptable?
items.text: The single most important question. *“100 per minute”* and *“no more than 100 in any 60-second span”* are different systems, and only one of them tolerates 100 arriving at once.

items.title: What happens on rejection — drop, queue, or 429?
items.text: Queuing turns a limiter into a scheduler, which is a different problem. Confirm you are rejecting.

items.title: One process, or many?
items.text: Single-process is a data-structure question. Distributed is a consensus question. Ask before you start.

items.title: Is approximate acceptable?
items.text: Almost always yes, and it buys you the cheap algorithms. Get it agreed.

blocks.caption: Every one of these is a legitimate answer. Choosing without naming the flaw is not.
rows: O(1) — a counter and a timestamp
**2× the limit at a boundary.** 100 at 11:59:59 and 100 at 12:00:00
Exact, and the memory is the problem: 10k/min per client is 10k timestamps
Approximates by weighting the previous window. Good default
Bursts up to the bucket size. Usually a feature, not a bug

blocks.title: The fixed-window boundary problem
blocks.caption: A limit of 100 per minute admits 200 requests inside one second, because the counter resets on a wall-clock boundary rather than relative to the traffic.

blocks.text: Token bucket — the one to reach for

Tokens refill at a constant rate; each request spends one. Empty bucket means rejection. It is O(1) in time and space, needs no timer thread, and it expresses burst tolerance as a number you can tune.

blocks.title: `nanoTime`, never `currentTimeMillis`
blocks.text: Wall-clock time goes backwards — NTP corrections, daylight saving, a VM resuming from a snapshot. A limiter that computes elapsed time from wall clock can produce a negative interval and hand out unlimited tokens. `System.nanoTime()` is monotonic; use it and say why.
LeetCode 359 is the degenerate case — limit of one per key per ten seconds — and it has one real trap.

blocks.title: This map never shrinks
blocks.text: One entry per distinct message, forever. Interviewers ask *“what happens after a billion unique messages?”* and the answer is an OOM. Fixes: an LRU bound on the map, a periodic sweep of entries older than the window, or a bucketed queue of keys to expire. **Volunteering this before being asked is the whole point of the question.**

items: `synchronized` per bucket is usually enough — buckets are per client, so contention only happens within one client's traffic.
A single global lock serialises every client and is the common mistake.
For a genuinely hot key, an atomic compare-and-swap loop on a packed `(tokens, timestamp)` long avoids the monitor entirely.
`ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent` for bucket creation, or two threads create two buckets for one client and each gets the full limit.

blocks.text: The moment there are two servers, per-process limiters give each client N × servers. The options, in ascending cost:

rows: Divide the limit by server count
A routing constraint, and rebalancing breaks it
A network hop on every request, and a new SPOF
Lease N tokens locally, refresh periodically. What most production systems do

blocks.title: The sentence that lands
blocks.text: *“In one process I would use a token bucket for the burst control. Across a fleet I would lease tokens from Redis in batches rather than checking centrally per request — it trades exactness for one fewer network hop on the hot path, and rate limits are a control, not an accounting system.”*

items.title: Different limits per tier
items.text: Free versus paid. The bucket's capacity and refill rate become per-client config, which is why they are fields and not constants.

items.title: Bound the memory
items.text: The unbounded-map problem, above. An LRU over buckets, evicting clients idle longer than one window.

items.title: Tell the caller when to retry
items.text: A token bucket knows exactly when the next token arrives, so `Retry-After` is computable rather than guessed. Nice detail to volunteer.

items.title: Never reject a paying customer
items.text: Queue instead of drop, with a bounded queue and a deadline. Say clearly that this is no longer a rate limiter.

items.title: Limit by cost, not count
items.text: Expensive endpoints spend more tokens. The bucket already supports it — spend *k* instead of 1.

blocks.text: Edge cases to state before you are asked

items: First request from an unseen client — bucket starts full, so the first burst is allowed. Confirm that is intended.
Clock going backwards → monotonic time makes this impossible rather than merely unlikely.
A limit of zero → reject everything, without dividing by zero in the refill.
A process paused for an hour → lazy refill caps at capacity, so it does not release an hour of tokens at once.
Two threads creating a bucket for the same new client → `computeIfAbsent`, not get-then-put.

rows: Names all four and what each gets wrong
Notices the leak before being asked
Local leases, and names the accuracy traded

blocks.title: The 45-minute plan
blocks.text: **0–5** clarify burst tolerance and single versus multi process. **5–12** the four algorithms and their failure modes — this is the highest-value ten minutes. **12–25** code the token bucket. **25–32** concurrency and the unbounded-map fix. **32–45** distributed, landing on local leases.
